analysis.one_liner: Applies Social Security payroll taxes to all earnings and ties retirees' inflation adjustment to senior spending.
analysis.headline: Introduced August 2025 with 12 Democratic sponsors and referred to three House committees, where no action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would apply the 12.4% Social Security payroll tax to all wages and self-employment income, phasing it in from 2026 to 2031; today, earnings above $176,100 (the 2025 cap) are exempt [S2]. It also computes a small additional benefit for people who paid taxes on earnings above that cap [S2]. Separately, it would switch Social Security's cost-of-living adjustment to an index that tracks the spending of people 62 and older, whose budgets weigh health care more heavily, and it would ensure any resulting benefit increase cannot push someone off Medicaid or Supplemental Security Income [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees, survivors, and disability beneficiaries gain from a cost-of-living adjustment built around what seniors actually buy, which typically rises faster than the standard index because of medical costs [S2]. Low-income beneficiaries gain because higher benefits could not cost them Medicaid or SSI eligibility [S2]. Social Security's finances also improve, since taxing all earnings raises more revenue for the same benefit promises [S2]. People who earn above the current cap would see a small additional benefit of their own (3% of most above-cap earnings, 0.25% of the highest earnings) [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Switches the annual cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security benefits to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which reflects the spending patterns of people 62 and older [S2][S3].
Bars any benefit increase from the new index from being counted as income for Medicaid or Supplemental Security Income eligibility or payment amounts [S2][S3].
Phases out the taxable maximum for payroll taxes between 2026 and 2031, after which all wages and self-employment income are subject to Social Security taxes [S2][S3].
Credits earnings above the cap into the benefit formula at a modest rate, so newly taxed high earners receive some additional benefit in return [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Workers whose wages exceed the taxable maximum would pay the 12.4% combined employee share on their full earnings, phased in over six years [S2][S3]. Their employers would owe the matching 6.2% on those same wages [S3]. Self-employed people above the cap would owe the full 12.4% themselves [S3]. High earners receive only a small offsetting benefit bump in the formula [S3].

drawbacks.text: The tax reaches the highest earners most: someone earning $1 million a year would eventually pay tens of thousands of dollars more in payroll taxes each year, a direct income hit to top earners and an added cost on their employers [S3].

High earners do not get benefits proportional to the new taxes. The bill credits above-cap earnings at roughly 3% and 0.25% rates, far below the ~15% marginal replacement rates the standard formula applies to ordinary earnings, so the tax increase is not matched one-for-one by benefits [S3].

Applying the employer half of the payroll tax to high salaries raises the cost of highly compensated labor, which good-faith critics argue could show up as slower pay growth or fewer high-end positions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go to people with modest fixed incomes — bigger, more accurate inflation adjustments that cannot claw back Medicaid or SSI — while the costs fall entirely on high earners and their employers, and the added revenue strengthens the program everyone depends on. The strongest honest objection is that high earners pay full payroll tax rates for only a token benefit in return; supporters would answer that Social Security was never designed as a dollar-for-dollar annuity and that progressivity is the point. On balance, the costs are concentrated at the very top and the benefits are broad.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2025 and sent to three House committees, and none of them has taken it up yet.

narrative.text: Representative Jill Tokuda introduced the bill on August 12, 2025, joined by seven original cosponsors [S3].
The Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Energy and Commerce and Education and Workforce Committees [S5].
As of the latest recorded action, no committee has held a hearing or markup and the bill has not received a floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. The bill sits unreferred-to-floor in committee; if it stays there, the people better off would be high earners and employers above the cap, who avoid the new tax.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet — bill is still parked in committee

sides.party_line_note: All 12 supporters — the sponsor and 11 cosponsors — are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the House committees involved are led by Republicans who have not acted on the bill.

industries.industry: High earners (wages above the $176,100 cap) and self-employed high earners
industries.note: They would pay the full 12.4% payroll tax on all earnings, phased in through 2031, receiving only a small offsetting benefit in the formula. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against the retirees and disabled beneficiaries it would fund.

Employers owe the matching 6.2% payroll tax on wages that today escape the cap, raising the cost of six- and seven-figure compensation. Cheaper high-end pay is their interest, not their workers' benefits.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has the typical profile of a measure that stalls: minority-party sponsorship only, three committee referrals splitting jurisdiction, and no recorded committee action months after introduction. Expect it to remain in committee unless Social Security financing becomes a negotiated priority; similar cap-elimination proposals have historically not reached a floor vote without bipartisan buy-in.
